content: Prior to the advent of modern medicine, many mothers and their babies did not survive pregnancy and childbirth. However, with advancements in medical care, proper prenatal care can now significantly enhance the quality of pregnancy and improve outcomes for both the infant and the mother. Effective prenatal care involves several key components: Maintaining good nutrition and healthy habits both before and during pregnancy. Attending regular prenatal examinations to monitor the health of the mother and baby. Undergoing routine ultrasounds to identify any potential issues with the baby. Participating in routine screenings for various conditions, including: Blood pressure abnormalities. Blood type incompatibilities, such as Rh and ABO issues. Diabetes. Genetic disorders, particularly if there is a family history or the mother’s age increases the risk. Rubella immunity. Sexually transmitted infections. Urine protein levels. Women who plan to carry a pregnancy to term should select a healthcare provider who will oversee their prenatal care, delivery, and postpartum services. Common provider options include: Obstetricians and gynecologists (OB/GYNs). Certified nurse midwives (CNMs). Family medicine physicians. Family nurse practitioners (FNPs) or physician assistants (PAs) working in collaboration with a doctor. Perinatologists, who specialize in managing very high-risk pregnancies. Family healthcare providers or generalists are equipped to manage normal pregnancies and deliveries. If complications arise during pregnancy, the primary doctor will refer the patient to a specialist. Folic acid supplementation is essential during pregnancy. A daily intake of 4 milligrams (400 micrograms) of folic acid is recommended to reduce the risk of certain birth defects, such as spina bifida. In cases where a woman has a higher-than-normal risk of these conditions, higher doses of folic acid may be prescribed. Pregnant women are advised to avoid all medications unless deemed necessary and recommended by their prenatal healthcare provider. It is crucial to discuss all medication use with the provider. Additionally, pregnant women should abstain from alcohol and drug use, limit caffeine intake, and refrain from smoking. They should also avoid herbal preparations and over-the-counter medications that could interfere with the baby’s normal development. Prenatal visits are typically scheduled as follows: Every 4 weeks during the first 28 weeks of gestation. Every 2–3 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks of gestation. Weekly from 36 weeks until delivery. During each visit, the healthcare provider usually measures and records the mother’s weight gain, blood pressure, fundal height, and the baby’s heartbeat (as appropriate). Routine urine screening tests may also be performed. It is important to seek urgent medical care in the following situations: If you suspect you are pregnant, are currently pregnant but not receiving prenatal care, or are unable to manage common pregnancy-related complaints without medication, schedule an appointment with a healthcare provider. If you suspect you are pregnant and are taking medications for conditions such as diabetes, thyroid disease, seizures, or high blood pressure, contact your healthcare provider. Notify your healthcare provider if you are pregnant and have been exposed to sexually transmitted infections, harmful chemicals, radiation, or unusual pollutants. If you are pregnant and develop a fever, chills, or painful urination, contact your healthcare provider. Immediate medical attention is required if you are pregnant and experience any of the following: Vaginal bleeding of any amount. Severe abdominal pain. Physical or severe emotional trauma. Rupture of membranes (water breaking). Additionally, if you are in the second half of your pregnancy and notice that the baby is moving less or not at all, contact your healthcare provider immediately.
